neighbours.label: the digits of the year of a named natural disaster ('the flood of 19|2|7', 'the earthquake of 19|0|6'): the date that identifies a catastrophe, as against the same years for ordinary events
fire: Many farms along the river were ruined by the flood of 1913 and never recovered.
The old cathedral collapsed during the earthquake of 1908 and was not rebuilt.
Fishermen on the coast still remember the hurricane of 1954 and the boats it sank.
The great storm of 1987 felled millions of trees across southern England.
Survivors of the tsunami of 1946 described a wall of water crossing the harbour.
The village was cut off for weeks after the blizzard of 1888 closed every road.
Records of the drought of 1934 show crops withering across the plains.
The wildfire of 1910 burned through three million acres of forest in two days.
quiet: Many farms along the river were bought by the railway company in 1913.
The old cathedral was consecrated by the bishop in 1908 after decades of work.
Fishermen on the coast formed their first cooperative in 1954 to sell their catch.
The great novel of 1987 was translated into twenty languages within a year.
Survivors of the class of 1946 met again for a reunion at the school.
The village opened its first post office in 1888 beside the church.
Records of the election of 1934 show a narrow win for the mayor.
The orchestra founded in 1910 gave its first concert in the town hall.

predictions: fire 0.4-0.6 on a year digit after 'the flood/earthquake/hurricane/blizzard of'; same years for births, foundings, publications below 0.05
notes: Card peaks on '9' in 'earthquake and fire of 1906', 'hurricane of 1944', 'Flood of 94'; promotes ' disaster', ' flood', ' hurricane', ' earthquake'. Probe: flood of 1927 0.572, earthquake of 1923 0.461, hurricane of 1938 0.395, blizzard of 1978 0.506; library founded in 1927 0.012, born in 1938 0.009, published in 1923 0.011. 'extreme heat event' and 'extreme sports event' both 0.267, so the ' extreme' card peak is not disaster-specific and is not used.
